questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Overshoot and collapse
questions.learningObjective: Identify overshoot and collapse from a described sequence.
questions.stem: Translator's note 21: The passage says a deer herd pushed past its habitat's capacity and then crashed. Which mechanism is being described?

options.text: Overshoot and collapse, because the herd grew beyond the food supply and the crash followed the excess
Maximum sustainable yield, because the herd's peak size was the largest the land ever carried
options.misconception: confuses a population peak with a sustainable harvest rate

options.text: Density-independent regulation, because the crash was caused by the herd leaving its usual range
options.misconception: blames movement rather than resource exhaustion

options.text: Delayed density dependence, because the crash came one year after the herd reached its peak
options.misconception: treats any lag as evidence of delayed density dependence

questions.explanation: Overshoot means the population grew beyond the habitat's resource limit and the collapse followed that excess. A peak size, a weather event, or a one-year lag do not establish the mechanism described.
questions.hint: Ask whether the herd exceeded what the land could feed.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Life expectancy from a cohort life table
questions.learningObjective: Compute life expectancy at birth from a cohort life table.
questions.stem: Translator's note 22: A cohort life table lists survivors l_x of 1000, 820, 640, 470, 310, 170 and 60 at ages 0 to 6, with none left at age 7. What is life expectancy at birth in years?
questions.explanation: Life expectancy at birth is person-years lived divided by the cohort size: 3470 / 1000 = 3.47 years. Dividing by the number of age classes, or averaging only the ages of those who died, misstates it.
questions.hint: Sum the survivors at each age, then divide by the cohort.

questions.topic: Mortality between two ages in a life table
questions.learningObjective: Write the interval mortality formula from a glossary definition.
questions.stem: Translator's note 23: A glossary entry says the mortality rate between ages x and x+1 is the fraction of the cohort alive at age x that dies before the next birthday. Which formula matches it?

options.text: The number of deaths in the year divided by the whole population, since mortality is a population-wide rate
options.misconception: divides by the whole population rather than the age cohort

options.text: The deaths between ages x and x+1 divided by the survivors at age x, since it is a conditional probability
The survivors at age x divided by the cohort at birth, since mortality is always measured against the start
options.misconception: uses the starting cohort as the denominator for all ages

options.text: The ratio of survivors at age x+1 to survivors at age x, since mortality is what remains alive
options.misconception: confuses the survival ratio with the mortality fraction

questions.explanation: The rate is conditional on surviving to age x, so it is deaths in the interval divided by those alive at age x. Dividing by the whole population or the starting cohort reverses it.
questions.hint: Mortality between ages is a conditional probability.

questions.topic: Net reproductive rate from a life table

questions.stem: Translator's note 24: A life table gives l_x m_x values of 0, 0, 1.200, 0.705, 0.310, 0.085 and 0 for a cohort of 1000 females. What is the net reproductive rate in daughters per female?
questions.explanation: The net reproductive rate sums l_x m_x over all ages: 1.200 + 0.705 + 0.310 + 0.085 = 2.3 daughters per female. Using only the largest litter, or dropping survival weights, misstates the total.
questions.hint: Add the survival-weighted fecundity across all ages.

questions.topic: Generation time from a life table
questions.learningObjective: Interpret generation time from a weighted life-table summary.
questions.stem: Translator's note 25: A table gives x l_x m_x values of 0, 0, 2.400, 1.930, 1.225, 0.425 and 0 for a cohort whose net reproductive rate is 2.3. What does the table say about generation time?

options.text: Generation time is 0.4 years, because the last cohort's share of the reproductive output is small
options.misconception: reads the smallest age-class contribution as the generation time

options.text: Generation time is 2.3 years, because the same number appears as the net reproductive rate
options.misconception: confuses the reproductive rate with the mean age of birth

options.text: Generation time is 2.6 years, because it is the age-weighted share of the reproductive output
Generation time is 6 years, because that is the last age at which the cohort reproduces at all
options.misconception: uses the maximum reproductive age instead of the mean

questions.explanation: Generation time divides the sum of x l_x m_x by R0: 5.98 / 2.3 = 2.6 years, the mean age of mothers producing the next cohort. Maximum reproductive age and R0 are different quantities.
questions.hint: Divide total x l_x m_x by the net reproductive rate.

questions.topic: Approximate growth rate from R0 and T
questions.learningObjective: Apply the approximate growth relation between R0 and T.
questions.stem: Translator's note 26: A life table summary gives a net reproductive rate of 3 and a generation time of 4 years. Apply the approximate growth relation to get r per year.
questions.explanation: The approximation is r = ln(R0)/T, so ln(3)/4 = 0.275 per year. Dividing R0 by T, or dropping the logarithm, overstates the rate because growth compounds.
questions.hint: Take the log of R0, then divide by T.

questions.topic: Growth rate solved from the renewal equation
questions.learningObjective: Read the solved rate from a plotted renewal sum.
questions.stem: Translator's note 27: A diagram shows the renewal sum plotted against the trial growth rate r: the curve starts above one at r = 0 and crosses the horizontal line at one at r = 0.7. What does the crossing point give?

options.text: The net reproductive rate, because the crossing shows how many young each female produces
options.misconception: confuses the crossing point with the reproductive output

options.text: The carrying capacity, because the crossing marks where the population stops growing
options.misconception: reads a rate solution as a capacity value

options.text: The intrinsic rate of growth, because the crossing shows where births exactly replace parents
options.misconception: describes the crossing without naming the solved rate

options.text: The intrinsic rate of increase, because that is the r for which the renewal sum equals one

questions.explanation: The renewal equation asks for the r at which the discounted sum of births equals one, where each generation replaces itself. That crossing is the intrinsic rate of increase, not a capacity.
questions.hint: The sum equals one at the solved growth rate.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Maximum sustainable yield on a logistic curve
questions.learningObjective: Design a stock assessment that estimates maximum sustainable yield.
questions.stem: Translator's note 28: Design a stock-assessment plan that estimates the maximum sustainable yield for a small commercial fishery.

answer.exemplar: Survey the stock with a consistent catch-per-unit-effort index across a series of years, recording both the adult biomass at the start of each season and the total removals. Plot the surplus production curve of removals against biomass and fit a logistic curve, so the biomass at the peak of the fitted curve gives the maximum sustainable yield directly. Repeat the estimate with the survey data split into early and late periods and check that the two estimates agree before reporting a single figure.

questions.explanation: Paired biomass and removals across a range of stock sizes are needed, since a yield curve cannot be built from removals alone. Fitting a logistic model and checking the peak across periods guards against one bad survey year.
questions.hint: Pair stock size with the removals taken from it.

questions.topic: Overshoot and collapse
questions.learningObjective: Correct an inference about carrying capacity from a decline.
questions.stem: Translator's note 29: A translator flags a sentence saying that because the reindeer population fell by half, the herd must have been at its carrying capacity. What is the error?

options.text: Falling numbers do not show the herd was at capacity, since an overshot population can collapse too
The error is that a halving of the population cannot be measured accurately in field counts
options.misconception: treats a counting error as the real problem

options.text: The error is that reindeer have no natural predators, so carrying capacity cannot be reached
options.misconception: reaches for an irrelevant predator argument

options.text: The error is that the sentence should describe the halving as a change in the finite rate of increase
options.misconception: thinks the fix is a different statistic rather than logic

questions.explanation: A decline is compatible with several explanations, including a population that overshot its food supply and then collapsed. Inferring capacity from the direction of change alone ignores the overshoot case.
questions.hint: A falling population does not locate the carrying capacity.

questions.topic: Life expectancy from a cohort life table
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a cohort life table from a static one.
questions.stem: Translator's note 30: A glossary distinguishes a cohort life table from a static one. Which statement about the cohort version is correct?

options.text: It assumes the mortality rates of the current year apply to all future years of life
options.misconception: describes the static life table as if it were the cohort one

options.text: It follows one real group of individuals from birth and records how many are still alive at each age
It is built from a single census year and applies that year's rates to a hypothetical cohort
options.misconception: confuses the cohort table with a current-year snapshot

options.text: It can only be built for humans, because other organisms cannot be followed from birth to death
options.misconception: restricts cohort tables to one taxon

questions.explanation: A cohort table follows a real group born together and records survivors at each age, describing a realised generation. A static table applies one year's rates to a hypothetical cohort.
questions.hint: One real group, followed over its whole life.

questions.topic: Mortality between two ages in a life table
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an interval mortality rate relates to a count of deaths.
questions.stem: Translator's note 31: A note on a deer life table asks why mortality between ages 4 and 5 is reported as 0.25 while 25 deer out of 100 are lost.

options.text: The 0.25 is a probability, while 25 of 100 is the observed count that estimates it
options.misconception: thinks a probability and an observed count must be identical

options.text: The 0.25 refers to the chance of dying at any age, while 25 deer reflects only the last age class
options.misconception: reads the interval rate as a whole-life mortality figure

options.text: The 0.25 is the proportion of the 100 alive at age 4 that die before age 5, the interval mortality
The 0.25 is the fraction of all deer lost over the whole life, while 25 deer covers only one interval
options.misconception: confuses a whole-life fraction with an interval rate

questions.explanation: Interval mortality conditions on survival to the start of the age class, so 25 deer lost from 100 alive at age 4 gives 0.25. Treating it as a whole-life fraction, or as the raw count, loses that conditioning.
questions.hint: Condition on the animals that reached age four.

questions.topic: Net reproductive rate from a life table
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a net reproductive rate of one from a life table.
questions.stem: Translator's note 32: A species' life table gives a net reproductive rate of 1.0, and the translation note explains what that means for the population over many generations.

options.text: The population will grow without limit, because a rate of one means every female leaves one daughter behind
options.misconception: reads one daughter per female as unlimited growth

options.text: The population will halve each generation, because the rate of one represents a fifty percent loss
options.misconception: confuses a replacement rate with a halving factor

options.text: The population size will stay exactly constant in every generation, because rates above and below one cancel
options.misconception: assumes individual generations average out to no change

options.text: The population is at replacement, since each female leaves one daughter on average over her life

questions.explanation: A net reproductive rate of one means each female leaves one surviving daughter on average, so the population is at replacement. That does not require identical generation sizes, only a long-run rate near zero.
questions.hint: One daughter per female means replacement, not growth.

questions.topic: Approximate growth rate from R0 and T
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the logarithm in the approximate growth relation.
questions.stem: Translator's note 34: A note explains the approximation r is about the natural log of R0 divided by T, and asks why the logarithm appears.

options.text: Because the growth rate applies continuously, so multiplying by r for each year compounds as an exponential
Because the log corrects for the fact that R0 is a ratio rather than a count of offspring
options.misconception: thinks the log is a units correction

options.text: Because the approximation was derived for populations with an exactly constant birth rate
options.misconception: claims a special birth-rate condition for the log

options.text: Because the log keeps the growth rate positive even when R0 is less than one
options.misconception: believes the log is needed to keep signs positive

questions.explanation: Growth at a continuous rate compounds, so a per-year change in the log of the population is what the approximation captures. The logarithm is not a units correction, nor a device for keeping signs positive.
questions.hint: A log converts a compounded factor into a constant rate.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Growth rate solved from the renewal equation
questions.learningObjective: Solve a simple renewal equation for the growth rate.
questions.stem: Translator's note 35: A life table gives survival-weighted births of 0.5 in the first year and 1.0 in the second, with nothing afterwards. For which growth rate does the renewal sum equal one?
questions.explanation: The renewal equation here is 1 = 0.5 + 1.0 e^(-r), so e^(-r) = 0.5 and r = ln 2, about 0.693 per year. Dropping the first term, or adding births without discounting, misreads the equation.
questions.hint: Rearrange so that the exponential term stands alone.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Maximum sustainable yield on a logistic curve
questions.learningObjective: Locate maximum sustainable yield on a surplus production curve.
questions.stem: Translator's note 36: A diagram shows surplus production on the vertical axis and stock size on the horizontal axis, with a bell-shaped curve peaking at the middle of the stock range. What does the peak represent?

options.text: The point where the stock is at its carrying capacity and the harvest should be zero
options.misconception: places the peak of the yield curve at carrying capacity

options.text: The maximum sustainable yield, which is reached when the stock sits at half its carrying capacity
The point where reproduction equals mortality and the population stops changing size
options.misconception: confuses the yield peak with the zero-growth point

options.text: The point of maximum population density, where crowding first limits individual survival
options.misconception: reads the yield peak as a crowding threshold

questions.explanation: On a logistic curve surplus production rN(1 - N/K) peaks where N equals K/2, and that peak rK/4 is the maximum sustainable yield. Carrying capacity lies where the curve meets the axis.
questions.hint: The yield peak sits at half the carrying capacity.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Overshoot and collapse
questions.learningObjective: Design a monitoring scheme that can detect overshoot and collapse.
questions.stem: Translator's note 37: Design a monitoring scheme that can detect an overshoot and collapse in a reindeer herd.

answer.exemplar: Survey the herd at regular intervals through the summer, recording total numbers, calf production and the condition of the plants the herd grazes, so that animal density and resource supply can be tracked separately. Continue the counts through the winter of any year in which numbers rise well beyond the long-term average, because a collapse would appear in the following count rather than in the year of the peak. Compare the timing of the animal peak with the timing of resource depletion, and check whether grazed vegetation recovers faster or slower than the herd rebounds.

questions.explanation: Detecting overshoot means following the herd past its peak, since the collapse is the diagnostic event and comes later. Tracking animals and vegetation together separates an overshoot from an ordinary slowdown.
questions.hint: Keep counting after the peak, and track the forage.

questions.learningObjective: Correct a definition of life expectancy at birth.
questions.stem: Translator's note 38: A draft says life expectancy at birth equals the age at which the last member of the cohort died. Identify the mistake.

options.text: There is no mistake, because the oldest survivor's age defines the cohort's life expectancy
options.misconception: confuses the maximum age with the mean

options.text: The mistake is that life expectancy can only be computed when the whole cohort has died out
options.misconception: claims the cohort must be complete before computing

The mistake is that the draft should have used the median age at death instead of the mean

questions.stem: Translator's note 39: A translation says that mortality is usually higher for the very young and the very old than for the middle ages. Why is that so?

options.text: Because young and old individuals have smaller body size, so they are more easily carried away by currents
options.misconception: invents a size-based cause for the age pattern

options.text: Because the young and the old are counted less often in the surveys that build the life table
options.misconception: attributes the pattern to survey effort

options.text: Because populations naturally concentrate at the two ends of the age range in most species
options.misconception: confuses the age pattern with the age structure

options.text: Because early life has high juvenile mortality and later life carries the accumulated risks of ageing

questions.explanation: Survivorship curves show high mortality early in life and a second rise in old age, the familiar U-shaped pattern. Body size and survey effort do not explain a rate drawn from cohort deaths.

questions.stem: Translator's note 40: A note asks what a net reproductive rate below one implies for a population over the long term.

options.text: The population declines over generations, because each female leaves fewer than one surviving daughter
The population stabilises at a smaller size, because a rate below one balances births against deaths exactly
options.misconception: treats a sub-unit rate as a stable equilibrium

options.text: Nothing can be concluded, because the net reproductive rate ignores the ages at which reproduction occurs
options.misconception: claims the rate is uninformative about population change

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mortality between two ages in a life table
questions.learningObjective: Design a study that measures mortality between two ages.
questions.stem: Translator's note 47: Design a study that measures mortality between two ages in a fish population.

answer.exemplar: Tag a large random sample of fish at the start of the season, recording the number tagged and the size distribution of the tagged fish, then use the proportion of tagged fish that are never seen again in subsequent recaptures to estimate survival between the two sampling occasions. Because recapture-based survival confounds emigration with death, pair the tagging work with an independent check of whether the fish can leave the area, for example by acoustic tags on a subset that are tracked continuously. Repeat the procedure across several ages so that the interval rates can be reported separately for each age class rather than pooled.

questions.explanation: Interval mortality requires following known individuals and detecting losses while separating death from emigration. Without that separation the rate is biased, and pooling across ages hides the age pattern.
questions.hint: Track known animals and separate death from departure.

questions.stem: Translator's note 48: A draft computes the net reproductive rate by adding up the litter sizes of every female without any survival adjustment. Identify the error.

questions.learningObjective: Design a monitoring plan that tests whether a fishery is at its maximum yield.
questions.stem: Translator's note 68: Design a monitoring plan that tests whether a coastal fishery is currently being fished at its maximum sustainable yield.

answer.exemplar: Set a regular monitoring schedule with the same survey method each year, recording the spawning stock biomass at the start of the season, the total catch taken, and the effort used, so that removals and stock size are paired across a wide range of biomass. Fit a surplus production model to those pairs and locate the biomass at which the fitted curve peaks, then compare the actual annual removals with the fitted maximum sustainable yield at the observed biomass. Repeat the comparison for several years and report how often removals exceed the modelled surplus, since a sustainable fishery should stay at or below it in most years.

questions.explanation: Testing the claim needs paired stock size and removals over enough years to fit a yield curve. Comparing each year's removals with the surplus the curve predicts at that stock shows whether the harvest is sustained.
questions.hint: Pair stock size with removals year by year.

questions.topic: Overshoot and collapse
questions.learningObjective: Design a study that detects overshoot in a grazed grassland population.
questions.stem: Translator's note 77: Design a study that shows whether a grazed grassland population overshot its carrying capacity.

answer.exemplar: Establish permanent quadrats across the grassland and record both the density of the grazing animals and the biomass and cover of the preferred forage species at the same dates each year, so that animal numbers and plant supply can be compared directly rather than separately. Keep a set of ungrazed reference quadrats and a set protected with exclosures as controls. If animal numbers in the grazed plots rise above the level at which forage was already exhausted, and the crash that follows coincides with forage recovery, the population is recorded as having overshot; a decline that appears while forage remains abundant points to another mechanism.

questions.explanation: Detecting overshoot means measuring animal density and resource supply together, and seeing whether the animal peak comes after the resource limit is reached. Control plots separate grazing effects from weather and plant change.
questions.hint: Measure animals and forage on the same plots.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Life expectancy from a cohort life table
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that life expectancy equals the number of age classes.
questions.stem: Translator's note 78: A draft says the life expectancy of a cohort is the number of age classes in the life table, and criticises a table with seven classes for giving a value of 3.69. Identify the mistake.

options.text: There is no mistake, because the number of age classes bounds the life expectancy exactly
options.misconception: believes the class count equals life expectancy

options.text: Life expectancy is person-years lived per cohort member, not the number of age classes, so 3.69 is correct
The draft is right to object, because life expectancy must be reported as a whole number of years
options.misconception: insists on whole-year life expectancy

options.text: The draft is right to object, because a life table cannot cover more than five age classes
options.misconception: invents a limit on the number of age classes

questions.explanation: Life expectancy averages the years each member lived, so it is the sum of the survivor column over the cohort size, 1845 / 500 = 3.69 years. Counting age classes measures the table's detail, not the lifespan.
questions.hint: Life expectancy is person-years per individual.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Mortality between two ages in a life table
questions.learningObjective: Explain why mortality rises in the oldest age class.
questions.stem: Translator's note 79: A translator asks why the mortality rate between two ages is often higher for the oldest animals in a cohort than for the middle ones.

options.text: Because the oldest animals have been counted more times, so their loss is more likely to be recorded
options.misconception: blames recording effort for the age pattern

options.text: Because mortality in the oldest class is divided by a smaller number, so any loss looks larger
options.misconception: explains the pattern by a denominator effect

options.text: Because senescence raises the chance of dying once an animal is past the age of maturity
Because predators preferentially take the oldest and slowest individuals in every population
options.misconception: assumes predation causes senescence everywhere

questions.explanation: Survivorship curves show a second rise in mortality in the oldest age class, the pattern called senescence. Recording effort, a smaller denominator and predation do not generate that rise in the death rate.
questions.hint: Look for the second drop on a survivorship curve.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Net reproductive rate from a life table
questions.learningObjective: Compute the net reproductive rate from survival-weighted fecundity.
questions.stem: Translator's note 80: A life table gives l_x m_x values of 0, 0.40, 0.90, 0.60 and 0.30 for a cohort of 1000 females. Apply the sum formula to find the net reproductive rate.
questions.explanation: The net reproductive rate sums l_x m_x over all ages: 0.40 + 0.90 + 0.60 + 0.30 = 2.2 daughters per female. Using only the largest class value, or adding raw litter sizes without survival weights, differs.
questions.hint: Add every survival-weighted fecundity value.
